body: Memo of 13 Aug 2025. Observations: about half the S&P 500's 58% two-year return in 2023-24 came from the Magnificent Seven, which reached ~one-third of index value; their average P/E ~33 he did not find unreasonable given 'exceptional products, significant market shares, high incremental profit margins, and strong competitive moats.' But fundamentals looked 'less good overall than they were seven months ago' (tariffs) while prices were higher; S&P +14% in the four months after 1 Apr 2025. A P/E 'is basically the result of applying a discounted cash flow calculation' with inputs growth, durability and ROIC; today's index is faster-growing, less cyclical, less capital-intensive - so 'it's different this time' is a cliche that 'always bears scrutiny' yet failing to see real change 'stands between the average investor and superiority.' Verdict: 'the stock market has moved from "elevated" to "worrisome."' INVESTCON scale: '6. Stop buying; 5. Reduce aggressive holdings and increase defensive holdings; 4. Sell off the remaining aggressive holdings; 3. Trim defensive holdings as well; 2. Eliminate all holdings; 1. Go short.' He says 3-2-1 are essentially never justified ('"overvaluation" is never synonymous with "sure to go down soon"'), and called for INVESTCON 5. Actionable: a graded, reversible response to high temperature - tilt, don't exit.
title: Marks Aug-2025 'The Calculus of Value': market moved from 'elevated' to 'worrisome'; the INVESTCON defensive ladder

body: Kahneman, Sibony and Sunstein, 'Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment' (2021): separate bias (systematic error) from noise (unwanted variability between judges, or within one judge over time). In a 'noise audit' at an insurer, executives expected about a 10% difference between two underwriters pricing the same case; the median difference was about 55%. Similar variability appears in sentencing, medicine, patent examination and investment valuation. Remedies, termed 'decision hygiene': structure the judgment into independent sub-assessments (the 'mediating assessments protocol'), score each separately before forming a holistic view, aggregate independent judges, use relative rather than absolute scales, and delay intuition until the end. Haynes et al., 'A Surgical Safety Checklist to Reduce Morbidity and Mortality in a Global Population' (New England Journal of Medicine 360, 2009; ~5,400 citations): the WHO 19-item checklist in 8 hospitals in 8 countries (nearly 7,700 patients) cut deaths from 1.5% to 0.8% and inpatient complications from 11% to 7%. That is evidence that checklists catch routine omissions experts already know about. Replicated: checklist results replicated in many systems (with weaker effects where compliance is poor). Noise-audit findings come from consulting studies and are less peer-reviewed. Use for us: (1) run every candidate through the same written checklist (disqualifiers, forensic flags, base-rate class, valuation), scored before reading bullish sell-side notes; (2) score sub-components independently and combine mechanically; (3) periodically re-score an old name blind to detect our own noise; (4) checklists are for avoiding omissions, not for generating ideas.
title: Noise and checklists: underwriters disagreed by 55% vs 10% expected (Kahneman-Sibony-Sunstein 2021); a 19-item checklist cut surgical deaths from 1.5% to 0.8% (Haynes 2009)
